description.p: Cairn (formerly nailong) is a lightweight Minecraft: Java Edition launcher written in Rust. Choose a Minecraft version and Fabric, NeoForge, Forge or vanilla, watch the install progress, and launch the game with an offline account. Incomplete downloads are detected and can be repaired.
It ships as a single native executable with no bundled runtime and keeps the launcher itself small.
Snapshots no longer skip files over 512 MB. Large files are backed up and restored in chunks without loading them into memory.

Saves page: while a snapshot, restore or prune runs, Back up all, Prune and Delete world are disabled too, and the busy status has its own line. Long data folder paths are shortened so Open folder and Refresh stay visible. Snapshots made in the same millisecond sort correctly.

Fixes: animations no longer stall and keep the CPU busy on slow frames; clicks during page transitions no longer hit the hidden new page; error messages no longer cover the bottom of the page or sit above dialogs; deleting a snapshot during a backup no longer freezes the window, and pruning runs in the background; the Linux update check no longer blocks the interface.

Flagship flat-matte Fog Craft polish and interaction pass while keeping 0% idle CPU, zero new dependencies, WCAG AA contrast across all semantic accents, and full reduce-motion support: key-gated critically-damped springs (zero scroll/resize lag) expanded to Versions list, Install loader tiles, Saves world list, Settings segmented controls, and lightbox filmstrip; full-viewport 220ms Dark/Light theme luminance cross-fade; floating animated bottom toasts; dual-region transitions for library status filters and Discover categories plus smooth lightbox photo cross-sliding; crisp 1.3px monochrome vector glyphs, 1px top rim edges, muted semantic loader pills, architectural matte monograms, real world icon.png previews, and keycap shortcuts.

Returns to the clean matte minimalist Fog Craft aesthetic (removing the 0.47.0 glossy gradients and scenic hero banner) while introducing a true dual-page paint-list transition compositor: outgoing pages glide out and dissolve smoothly alongside incoming pages with staggered Shared-Axis curves and zero layout reflow across primary navigation, drill-ins, in-page panes, and tabs; fixes monotonic-clock critically-damped springs for gliding sidebar/tab/palette indicators and toggle switches across 60–240Hz displays; adds unified open and close animations to all modals and popovers while maintaining 0% idle CPU and reduce-motion support.

Alpine Horizon visual overhaul (Dark "Alpine Dusk" & Light "Alpine Morning") while maintaining 0% idle CPU, zero extra dependencies, and WCAG AA contrast: GPU-cached procedural atmospheric backdrop and panoramic alpine-ridge Home hero stage; luminous gradient primary buttons and progress bar; upgraded Observatory status ring with ambient aura and jewel core; asymmetric Bento summary cards with real world icon.png or procedural biome thumbnails and colored icon badges; custom loader brand emblems across Versions and Install; translucent glass cards across Content, Saves, Gallery, Progress, and color-coded Command Palette.

Fixed Linux auto-update vs manual update lock conflict: disable the manual Update button while cairn-update.service is actively running, check systemd unit state before invoking pkexec, add DPkg::Lock::Timeout=30 to apt-get install, and clear stale install errors whenever the updated binary is ready on disk so "installed, restart to apply" and a lock error can never appear together.

Fog Craft UI overhaul across Dark and Light themes while keeping 0% idle CPU and WCAG AA contrast: five-level matte slate-fog elevation palette and 7/10/12 corner radius scale; recessed sidebar with geometric 3-stone Cairn mark, built-in Ctrl+K quick-search bar, and active indicator rail; redesigned Home 3-card summary, unified segmented launch spec bar, and refined status ring with clamped tooltips; clearer segmented and underlined Content tabs, baseline-aligned Discover cards with crisp install buttons; vertical snapshot backup timeline on Saves; Raycast-style Command Palette with keycaps; unified elevated modal frames across all dialogs.

Windows console popup fix and UI copy cleanup: apply CREATE_NO_WINDOW to Forge/NeoForge installer processors and Java runtime probing so installing versions on Windows no longer flashes black console windows; trimmed verbose boilerplate and fixed three stale UI hints across all pages and dialogs.

Reliability and polish pass: atomic file writes now use collision-free temp names and create credential files with 0600 permissions immediately on Unix; snapshot restore, delete and chunk-map reads now share the repository lock with backup and prune; non-install errors (login, saves, snapshots, updates) no longer carry a misleading install-failure prefix; Windows self-update handles locked backup executables more cleanly. Refreshed all documentation screenshots to Cairn 0.45.1 and moved full release history into CHANGELOG.md.

World snapshots are stored per chunk, and a chunk map lets you roll back just the chunks you select, with terrain, entities and POI together and a safety snapshot first. Pruning no longer breaks snapshots of deleted worlds. Cancel stops only the current task. First Forge/NeoForge install downloads Java when needed. Fixes for Windows paths, native library extraction, cleanup sizes, login and GC logs.

A running game no longer blocks the launcher: the sidebar shows each session, a stuck game can be ended, and different versions can run side by side. Start straight into a world. After a crash, undo the content changes made since the last good session in one step. Ctrl+K finds versions, worlds, pages and settings. Duplicate versions, drop worlds in to import them, play time tracking, tabbed settings, interface zoom, and the window and selected version are remembered.

Export any version as a minimal .mrpack: mods, resource packs and shaders available on Modrinth or CurseForge are saved as download links, and everything else is packed. Cairn can now use the .minecraft folder of other launchers such as PCL, HMCL or the official launcher, with accounts and settings carried over.

Rows and cards respond wherever you click, including on their text. Everything clickable shows a pointing hand and darkens when pressed. Version rows have a right-click menu and can be switched with the arrow keys. Error messages can be copied. The version number now shows in the bottom-right corner.

Faster mod downloads: one shared connection pool, dependencies resolved in parallel, update checks run in parallel, and up to 32 files download at once. Downloads and installs no longer lock the launcher; a card in the sidebar shows progress. The progress page shows one overall percentage and total time left. Dropping files in no longer freezes the window: restore points run in the background and skip unchanged files.

Cairn checks for updates only when it opens; nothing runs on a schedule. On Linux, when a new version is found, it is installed in the background from Cairn's apt repository without a password prompt. The hourly timer added in 0.42.2 is removed on upgrade.

Updates arrive sooner. Cairn checks for a new version every time it opens and every two hours while open. On Linux the deb adds an hourly timer that upgrades only the cairn package from its own repository, instead of waiting for the daily system upgrade.

Imports Prism Launcher and MultiMC instance exports that sit inside one folder or carry their own component patches and libraries. Old version files now get the native library path at launch, and automatic memory tuning recognizes loaders from the libraries when a pack uses its own main class.

One folder per version. Each version is a single folder with a complete version file and its own mods, worlds and config, so deleting one never breaks another. Name versions when installing and rename them later; the same loader can be installed several times. Deleting moves the folder to the trash. Modpacks install as a version folder too. Settings can clean up libraries and assets no version uses.

Automatic updates. On Windows, new versions download in the background and are swapped in when Cairn closes. On Linux, the deb adds Cairn's apt repository, so the system updates Cairn daily; Cairn can also be installed with apt directly.
The initial heap now always equals the maximum heap. When free memory is too low for ZGC to reserve the whole heap, automatic tuning uses G1 for that launch.

Multiple accounts: Microsoft, external login (authlib-injector, e.g. LittleSkin) and offline, switched from the sidebar. Passwords are not stored. New Screenshots page with overview, time, place and people views. Screenshots taken in games started from Cairn record the world or server and the player in the PNG text chunk. The viewer can zoom, pan, set a world icon and move files to the trash.

Downloads now fall back to community mirrors when the official servers do not answer: BMCLAPI for Minecraft and mod loader files, MCIM for the Modrinth and CurseForge APIs. A failed host is remembered for five minutes so the rest go straight to the mirror, every file is still checked against the official hashes, and API keys are never sent to a mirror. Settings can choose official-first or mirror-first, credits both mirrors, and the Content page says when a mirror is in use.

The download page now shows the finished steps, the files just downloaded, the source (Mojang or the BMCLAPI mirror), speed and time left. When no suitable Java is installed, Cairn downloads Mojang's official runtime and then launches the game. A quiet update check shows a badge when a new version is out, with release notes and a verified download. The interface code is reorganised into modules per page and dialog.

Renamed to Cairn (formerly nailong); the Linux data directory moves over automatically and the deb replaces the old package. Home now shows the launch settings this version will use and opens per-version settings for Java, memory, collector, JVM flags and window size with a copyable command-line preview. A screenshot wall on Home opens images on left click and copies them to the clipboard on right click. Installed content opens instantly from a cache that only re-reads changed files, long version names are shown in full, and the Windows exe has an icon and version information.

Tuning is split in two. A one-click machine test runs a small built-in Java workload that mimics the game, without a game window, and compares G1 and ZGC on every Java 21+ in a standard and a large-modpack tier; the verdict is shared by every version. Memory is learned from real play: each session's GC log tells the launcher how much data stays live in your world. The content page gains clickable status filters, a real search box, drag and drop from the file manager, and Open folder; a new log window opens this run's game output directly with the likely cause on top.

Tuning benchmark: one click builds a separate test instance, quick-plays into a built-in test world and flies through freshly generated terrain for two or three rounds to measure how much memory the version really needs and whether G1 or ZGC pauses less. Auto then launches with the measured values until mods, Java or installed memory change. Works for Minecraft 1.20 and later, including 26.x, without touching saves.

Fixes Minecraft 26.x: installation no longer fails on the new default-user-jvm section, and native libraries are found again at launch. Automatic tuning follows the official JVM defaults Mojang ships in 26.x version files. Java selection picks the lowest sufficient version and prefers OpenJDK over GraalVM.

Automatic JVM tuning: memory defaults to Auto and the heap size is calculated from physical and free memory, CPU threads, the Java version and the mod count. Tuned G1 flags by default, compact object headers on Java 25, and generational ZGC for large modpacks on strong machines. Settings shows the result, the reasoning and the full flag list; memory, collector and extra JVM arguments can still be set by hand.

Fog Blue interface: nailong's own minimal, matte look replaces the Minecraft-like pixel style, with dark and light themes that follow the system by default. A status ring on Home shows file integrity, every mod and world snapshots, with hover explanations, click-through and keyboard support. System CJK fonts replace the bundled pixel font. Idle CPU remains 0%.

Deepslate interface: a Minecraft-native pixel language with the bundled Fusion Pixel 12 px CJK face, zero rounded corners, two-pixel hard borders, beveled block buttons, pixel icons, a deepslate brick shell and a procedurally painted isometric voxel island on Home. All pages and dialogs share the same block components; the 900×620 layout hides the latest-world slot and status strip and scrolls Settings. Idle CPU remains 0%.

Aurora interface: a deep ink-blue glass shell, serif display type, procedural aurora/star/moon/dragon-constellation artwork generated in Rust and cached as textures, a poster-like Home with a hero and bento layout, restored four-column content grid, and a scrollable Settings dialog at 900×620. Idle CPU remains 0%.
Static ambient background: the gradients, dot grid and embers remain, but the window no longer redraws the whole page every 66 ms. Focused idle CPU under Xvfb/llvmpipe dropped from about 162% to 0%.
Reduce Motion: a persisted setting disables page fades, ambient animation, card lift, button movement and progress sheen while keeping colour and border feedback, and stops idle ambient repaints.
Keyboard paths: Ctrl+1–4 switch primary pages, Ctrl+, opens Settings, F5 refreshes versions. Shortcuts yield to text fields and open dialogs, with a discoverable hint in Settings.

Settings polish: a 1 GB memory stepper replaces the raw DragValue, the Java row shows the actual runtime with Recheck and a download link when missing, and name/memory/Java no longer share one crowded line.

Update confirmation: “Update all” and single-row updates show a checklist with each project’s from → to version, target instance, download size, old-file cleanup and the automatic restore point before writing anything.

Control consistency: version statistics put the number above its label, Auto Backup and Show Base Versions use the warm toggle switch instead of default checkboxes, and the Saves toolbar is ordered auto-backup → interval → keep → back up all → prune.

Failure states and dismissal polish: a failed login opens a dedicated result card with Retry and Close, Escape closes Settings, Account, Restore Points, login wait and login error, and content errors offer Reload. Raw OAuth details stay in the Settings log.

Interaction fixes: Windows login links are opened without cmd so the full OAuth query survives, cancelling login no longer poisons content browsing, and Home/version summaries are cached per page with a shorter transition. Content shows a skeleton while loading, and login errors are short and actionable.

Loader-aware restore points: version JSON and patched client jar inside an isolated version directory are stored with the content restore point and restored exactly. Reinstalling or repairing an existing loader takes a point first. Shared libraries are not copied, and world saves keep their separate snapshot system.

Install confirmation and first-launch onboarding: every content install now shows the target version, destination directory, file, size, dependencies and a restore-point note before writing; cancelling leaves disk untouched. First launch becomes a three-step guide for Java 21+, the game directory, and installing the first version or importing a modpack.

Instance content restore points: mods, configs, resource packs, shaders and the content index are stored in a deduplicated object store, snapshotted automatically before installs, updates, imports and deletes. The Content page gains a restore-point dialog with manual creation, verified restore and a safety point of the current state. World saves keep their own separate snapshot system.

The play-first product pass: the home screen is rebuilt around a single primary action and a recent world, while account, memory, Java, paths and logs move into a sidebar Settings dialog with persisted preferences. Decorative status rings, dashboard cards and quick-action clutter are removed from Home.

Typography and control polish: a real bold CJK family for headings, list titles and primary buttons, a matte amber primary action with optional play/download glyphs, and layered secondary buttons with warm borders and contact shadows.

A warm cream, yellow and orange light theme replaces the dark UI. A persistent sidebar now holds four top-level places: Home, Versions, Content and Saves. Content merges discovery and installed items into one library with mode tabs, and Saves becomes a first-class page with its own version picker instead of a subpage of version management. Install and detail pages get explicit local back paths, and the layout is rechecked down to 900×620.

The design system gained light and motion: ambient glows and drifting embers, card hover lift with accent borders, a page-transition veil, a breathing gradient primary action, an animated progress bar with a moving sheen, and modal fade-ins.

The launcher UI was rebuilt around one design system: a warm accent on a dark neutral palette, a fixed page header with a single scrolling content area, consistent cards, list rows, switches, popovers and empty states. The download center gained a redesigned browsing grid, a project page with install/version panels, and a real content manager with filtering, update banners, per-row updates and inline delete confirmation. Main, install, version manager, saves, progress and the account/login dialogs were rebuilt as well, and the whole app is responsive down to 900×620.

World backups became git-style snapshots: content-defined chunking with a shared object store, so only changed chunks are stored. Snapshots can be restored or deleted, pruned by count, and scheduled automatically every 15–120 minutes.

Download center targets an installed version explicitly and writes into that version's folder, with a browse-only mode. Version management gains per-version content and saves pages: list worlds, back them up to zip, restore and delete, plus enable/disable and open-folder actions for mods and resource packs.
The loopback probe now recognises the login_required redirect as success instead of treating every AADSTS response as a rejection.
The login probe now follows the whole redirect chain, so a missing loopback redirect URI is reported with an actionable message instead of failing later in the browser.
Login now probes the loopback redirect URIs registered in Azure and uses the one Microsoft accepts (usually http://localhost), and accepts the callback on the root path.

Microsoft account login via browser authorization code + PKCE: the launcher opens the Microsoft page, catches the loopback callback, walks MSA → Xbox Live → XSTS → Minecraft Services, stores the refreshing token with 0600 permissions, and launches with the real access token. Offline mode is unchanged.

Browsing no longer forces a Minecraft version or loader: pick any version or “all versions” (all loaders) and browse the whole catalogue without installing anything first. Cards now show a short description.
Category chips are capped at twelve with a “more categories” toggle, so the browse header stays compact.
Only top-level CurseForge categories are shown as chips by default, keeping the browse header compact.
CurseForge categories are fetched at runtime and rendered as native chips, with a source switch for All / Modrinth / CurseForge. Downloads still go through the launcher with verification.

Browse-first download center: category chips, popular and newest shelves, icon cards and one-click install of the latest compatible release with required dependencies. Search moved to the top bar and now renders the same cards.

Complete download center: mod, resource-pack and shader search with pagination, dependency planning, installed-content index with enable/disable/delete, duplicate detection, update checks and local imports.
Mod discovery for Fabric, NeoForge and Forge: search Modrinth and CurseForge, choose a compatible file, review required/optional dependencies, and download into a version-isolated mods directory.

CurseForge credentials are now built in and lightly obfuscated; the user-facing API key setting and local settings file were removed. Maintainers can still override the key with an environment variable.

Official builds include a project CurseForge API key so regular users can import CurseForge packs without configuring one. Runtime environment variables and user settings still take precedence; the embedded key is extractable and treated as a shared default quota.
Install cancellation: downloads, extraction and loader processors now respond to a cancel button; completed parts are kept for the next repair.

CurseForge compliance fixes: respect files whose authors disabled third-party distribution, use the official download page instead of synthesizing CDN URLs, space out metadata requests, and support an optional build-time default key.

The settings page can store a CurseForge API key for official file metadata, size and SHA1 verification. The key is masked, written to the data directory with owner-only permissions on Unix, and never logged.
Modpack imports now cover Modrinth, CurseForge, Prism/MultiMC, MCBBS, HMCL and ATLauncher, with optional CurseForge API hashes.
Modpack imports: Modrinth .mrpack, CurseForge manifest zip and Prism/MultiMC exports, with format detection and loader installation.
Downloader upgrades: four-way range download for large single files, resumable segment parts, cross-source fallback, and a 180-second transfer timeout.
Content-addressed patched-client reuse: scan existing launcher roots, verify, and hardlink instead of downloading the patch or running processors.
Parallel install pipeline: assets, client/libraries, loader patch and processors now run concurrently where dependencies allow.
Size-optimized release (about 7.6 MB), a machine-wide patch cache, and the version management from 0.4.3.

Loader base versions are hidden from the main picker, with a management page for deleting versions and instances. Reinstalling an intact loader is now instant, and the 3 MB core data is fetched in parallel.
Forge and NeoForge installs now fetch only the core installer data (about 3 MB) instead of the full 7–9 MB package; mirrors without range support fall back safely.
Fabric, NeoForge, Forge and vanilla installs, with version pickers, progress and repair.
